content: Alaria esculenta, commonly referred to as dabberlocks, badderlocks, or winged kelp, is an edible seaweed traditionally consumed along the coasts of the far northern Atlantic Ocean. It is one of the twelve species of the genus Alaria found in the British Isles. Description Alaria esculenta can grow to a maximum length of 2 meters. Its frond is characterized by a distinct midrib with wavy, membranous laminae on either side, each up to 7 cm wide. The frond is unbranched and tapers towards its distal end. At its base, the frond arises from a short stipe, which is attached to a rhizoidal holdfast. The stipe may bear several sporophylls, which are club-shaped structures measuring up to 20 cm in length and 5 cm in width. The entire frond is brown in color. The plant grows from a short, cylindrical stipe that anchors to rocks via a holdfast composed of branching, root-like rhizoids. The stipe extends into the frond, forming a prominent midrib. The lamina is thin, membranous, and has a wavy margin. Distribution and Ecology Alaria esculenta is widely distributed in the British Isles, except for the southern and eastern regions of England. It is a common large alga found on rocky shores exposed to severe wave action. It typically grows attached to rocks just below the low-water mark in the Laminaria belt and is prevalent in exposed coastal areas. Leaf-like sporophylls develop from the stipe and are responsible for producing zoospores. Global Distribution In Europe, Alaria esculenta is found in Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Norway, France, Helgoland, and the Netherlands. In North America, it is distributed along the coasts of Alaska, Labrador, and Massachusetts.
